title: The Magic Flute
facts: The Magic Flute premiered on 30 September 1791 in Vienna, just two months before Mozart’s death.
At the premiere Mozart conducted, the librettist Schikaneder played Papageno himself, and the Queen of the Night was sung by Mozart’s sister-in-law, Josepha Hofer.
Mozart to his wife on 7 October 1791: “I have this moment returned from the opera, which was as full as ever … what always gives me the most pleasure is the silent approval!”
Mozart went to hear his new opera almost every night, taking along friends and relatives.
The opera reached its 100th performance in November 1792, but Mozart didn’t live to see it: he died on 5 December 1791.
The overture was written after the rest of the opera. Its three solemn brass chords nod to Freemasonry, where the number three is highly significant.
Both Mozart and Schikaneder were Freemasons, and the opera is noted for its Masonic elements.
Papageno’s whistle is based on a motif borrowed from a concerto by Antonio Salieri.
The Papageno–Papagena duet, with its bird-like syllables, resembles a comic cavatina in Salieri’s Prima la musica e poi le parole.
Mozart called for a “stromento d’acciaio” (instrument of steel) to play Papageno’s magic bells.
The Armed Men’s chorale is set to a Baroque chorale prelude, inspired by Martin Luther’s hymn “Ach Gott, vom Himmel sieh darein”.
Pauline Kael called it “a peerlessly silly masterpiece: sublimely lucid music arising out of a parodistic fairy tale.”

Some see the Queen of the Night as a portrait of Empress Maria Theresa, who banned Freemasonry from Austria.
Early productions were often of highly altered, sometimes even mutilated, versions of the opera.
